articles.title: Companies are getting less accurate data on extreme weather just when they need it the most
articles.author: Suvrat Dhanorkar, Associate Professor of Operations Management, Georgia Institute of Technology
paras: The extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns – just to name a few examples.

But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather.

To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has been forecasting a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its October update put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027.
That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in.

But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters, which adds up costs weeks after the event, that NOAA stopped updating in May 2025. The Trump administration has also cut or undercut federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for daily forecasting, which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events – a risky prospect for businesses.

As a scholar of business operations and sustainability, I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices.
Gaps in climate science grow

In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts. The economic hit can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars.

This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the U.S. averaged fewer than five “billion-dollar” disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year – a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And the 2023 and 2024 totals were the highest on record.

While the scope of weather damage gets worse and worse, critical data is missing. That includes NOAA’s decision to retire its “Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters” database, ending updates after 2024.

For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U.S. weather disasters after the fact – and businesses and researchers alike have relied on it to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to put odds on future losses or to forecast economic activity. Some of my own research also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data.
Unfortunately, the gap in climate science may be widening.

In 2025 the federal government shut down Climate.gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U.S. government’s preeminent reports on climate science, were taken offline, while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites, which feed forecast models.

Fortunately, some of these data-gathering efforts have migrated elsewhere. The scientists behind the El Niño blog have moved to a nonprofit, while another nonprofit is carrying on the efforts behind the billion-dollar disaster database.
What this means for supply chains

The Trump administration has justified these cuts by citing high administrative costs and potential errors in the prediction models. But that still leaves companies, which lean on public weather data more than most shoppers realize, scrambling.

In many industries, including retail, food processing and agriculture, the payoff from acting early to safeguard supply chains can be large. Real-time and near-real-time data is used in supply chains for enhancing crop yields, finding the best routes for transport, inventory planning, and ensuring worker safety during weather emergencies. For example, Walmart invests heavily in technology and specialists to monitor weather-related disruptions and build resilient supply chains.

Another example is insurance companies, which use weather data for designing commercial insurance policies and processing claims. Risk Management Solutions Inc., a leading catastrophe risk-modeling company owned by Moody’s Corp., regularly use NOAA’s hurricane datasets to inform its advanced risk models.

When public climate data disappears, companies still need timely information to run their supply chains, so some will pay for alternative data. This typically comes from paid private services and subscriptions. Startups such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow.io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone offer private weather balloon data and advanced climate prediction services.

While privatization can fill some gaps, it’s usually only the large retailers and insurers who can afford these forecasts. Smaller suppliers, local farmers and independent truckers further up the supply chain often can’t.
And that’s exactly where many disruptions begin.
What it means for consumers

Shoppers feel these disruptions when shortages feed into higher prices, often months later. In 2024, for example, extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, pushed U.S. orange juice prices to an all-time high that fall. They have have stayed elevated since hurricanes Helene and Milton battered Florida’s groves.
Holiday staples are also not spared. A 2021 heat dome in the Pacific Northwest led to major damage to Christmas tree farms, causing their prices to rise an additional 5% to 10% that year.
And these effects are often global. Poor rains in West Africa more than doubled cocoa prices in 2024, and that inflation is still feeding into U.S. chocolate prices, which were up 14% in 2026.
A historic El Niño, arriving just as federal climate data becomes sparse, makes this winter an ideal, if unfortunate, test of what climate information is really worth.

articles.title: Doctors in Congress used to lean Republican – the 120th Congress marks a historic shift
articles.author: Michael E. Shepherd, Assistant Professor of Health Management and Policy, University of Michigan
paras: The 120th Congress, which will be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027, will have 20 physicians as members, along with twice that number of members who have other professional health backgrounds.

This physician class will make history for including the most Democratic physicians in a single Congress – 11 – in American history – a marked shift from the Republican dominance of previous physician members. These Democratic physicians made their professional expertise and their health policy ideas centerpieces of their campaigns, and now they have the opportunity to advance their health policy agendas.

I am a political scientist who studies the partisan politics of health and health policy in the U.S. While physicians have long shaped American health policy, the physician class elected to the upcoming Congress is the most Democratic in the modern era.

The Democratic physician class in the Senate includes South Carolina’s Annie Andrews, a pediatrician. Andrews made reproductive health and rural healthcare access core tenets of her campaign. For instance, her campaign website stressed that “As a doctor and a mom, I’ve cared for women in some of the most difficult moments of their lives. … I’ll fight to: Restore the protections of Roe v. Wade, Guarantee access to contraception and infertility care, Expand maternal health services, especially in rural areas.”

In the House of Representatives, the Democratic physician class includes California’s Richard Pan, also a pediatrician. Pan’s campaign website, which featured many pictures and references to his physician background and stressed the importance of holding “RFK accountable for endangering Americans” – referring to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. – as well as fighting to lower prescription drug costs, preventing the continued withering of the Affordable Care Act and banning prior authorization.

Other Democratic medical doctors who will be serving in the 120th Congress include two newly elected members in the House, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey and Amish Shah of Arizona, in addition to six returning representatives. Newly elected to the Senate alongside Andrews is Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, an epidemiologist with a medical doctorate.

Beyond Congress, Democratic medical doctors will also serve as governors – with Amy Acton newly elected in Ohio and Josh Green reelected in Hawaii – as well as in numerous state legislative positions.
Doctors’ long history in politics

Physicians have played important roles in shaping American politics and health policies, back to the nation’s founding. For instance, Pennsylvania’s Dr. Benjamin Rush, an early public health advocate who led the city of Philadelphia through the yellow fever epidemic of 1793, was the only person with a medical degree to sign the Declaration of Independence.

Since the late 1980s, the number of physicians serving in Congress has increased substantially term over term. My colleagues and I have documented this rise, as well as how physician members of the House have influenced policy.

We found that physician members of the House were more active and effective in enacting health policy than other members. Physician members were more likely to sponsor health legislation, and their health bills advanced further in the legislative process. This was true for physicians from both parties, both on and off congressional health-related committees.

Since at least 1973, when our data begin, physician House members’ congressional voting behaviors and their health policies have been more conservative than other members on average, even those of their own parties. For example, we found that physician members were more likely to sponsor bills related to curbing abortion access, repealing the ACA and protecting private sector physician autonomy.

However, one of the most striking changes we observed was the shift from the Republican dominance of physician members of Congress to the steadily increasing number of Democratic physicians elected since 2015. That year, there were just two Democratic physicians in Congress, but the 119th Congress – 2025-2027 – has six Democratic physicians. The upcoming Congress will nearly double that amount, with the largest class of Democratic members with medical doctorates in American history.

It will be the first Democratic physician majority since 1995, during the 103rd Congress, when two out of the three physician House members were Democrats. Before 1995, physician members were much rarer, but the majority of them were Republicans. Between 1995 and 2023, 80% of physician members were Republicans.
These partisan changes reflect the broader partisan shifts within the medical community itself.
For most of the 20th century, the majority of physicians – both in Congress and more generally as a group – were Republicans. The American Medical Association was largely a conservative organization.
The party loyalties of today’s physician class mirror the slowly shifting demographics of physicians as a group.
Since the 1970s – and especially since the 1990s – medical school applicants and new physicians have become more diverse in terms of gender, race and ethnicity.

These groups tend to identify as Democrats at higher rates, though medicine as a field continues to be dominated by white men. Additionally, becoming a physician obviously requires getting an undergraduate and a professional degree, but higher educational attainment alone has also become increasingly related to Democratic support.
Beyond these more glacial demographic changes, three Trump-era events have shaped the political mobilization of Democratic physicians.

First, the partisan politics of COVID-19 and especially the politicization of the COVID-19 vaccine, has been associated with decreasing trust in medicine and science from Republican-aligned voters and an increase in physicians’ Democratic support.

Second, the elevation of Kennedy as HHS secretary, whose own vaccine skepticism has long run contrary to medical science and the advice of physicians, further pitted many physicians against the Republican Party.

Finally, the Supreme Court’s decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health, which overturned the Constitutional right to abortion, also appears to have politically mobilized many OB-GYNs and other women’s health professionals in response to threats to the care they provide and their professional livelihoods.
All these factors have contributed to a new physician class in Congress that is more Democratic and liberal in their health policy views than previous years.

Ultimately, what this difference means for future public policy remains to be seen. However, if politicians’ campaign priorities portend their legislative activity, there may be a more active push than Congress has ever seen for health reforms related to reproductive healthcare, rural health, prescription drug pricing, bans on prior authorization requirements by health insurers and maybe even Medicare for all.

articles.title: Bloody, brutal and growing: More states are adopting the firing squad as an execution method
articles.author: Austin Sarat, William Nelson Cromwell Professor of Jurisprudence and Political Science, Amherst College
paras: The U.S. Army is scheduled to execute Nidal Hasan on Dec. 3, 2026, after Hasan killed 12 soldiers and one civilian at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth got President Donald Trump’s approval to use the firing squad to put Hasan to death.

However, the U.S. military hasn’t used the firing squad since 1945. And the execution method has been minimally used outside the military, accounting for only six of 1,664 executions in the U.S. in the past 50 years. Since 1976, the firing squad has been used in only two states: South Carolina and Utah.

The infrequency of its use might seem surprising to many Americans. After all, the firing squad is the least complicated execution method ever used in the U.S. All that is needed are guns, bullets and marksmen.

Still, it has not caught on throughout America’s history. And as a scholar of execution methods, I know why. Firing squad executions are bloody and brutal, and the U.S. has been more comfortable using methods that appear more humane.
History of firing squads in the US

The first use of a firing squad in what eventually became the U.S. occurred in 1608 in the English settlement of Jamestown. George Kendal, a British naval officer, was tried, convicted and sentenced to death for mutiny and treason. He was shot rather than hanged because of his high social standing. It was thought of as a more honorable way to die.

In 1996, a group of archaeologists found the skeleton of a young man in the walls of the original Jamestown fort, in what is modern-day Virginia. The skeleton showed signs of several gunshot wounds, and the archaeologists suspected it was Kendall’s remains.
The firing squad was used in the American Revolution to punish desertion. During the Civil War, both sides used it to create a “public spectacle, a vision of terror” to discourage desertion.

The U.S. Supreme Court in 1878 upheld the constitutionality of firing squad executions. Firing squads, the court decided, would not bring the sort of “terror, pain and disgrace” that would violate the Eighth Amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment.

Nonetheless, after the Civil War and into the early 20th century, the firing squad was used only in Utah and Nevada. In 1913, Nevada built a device that fired three guns by pulling strings. The move came after the state had trouble finding volunteers to serve on firing squads.
20th-century firing squad executions

In 1915, labor activist Joe Hill was put to death in Utah by firing squad after being convicted of murdering three people. Hill had been a very vocal critic of capitalism and what he called the “greedy master class.” Some of his sympathizers claimed he was murdered as much for his activism as for his crimes.

As The Salt Lake Tribune noted in 2015, “Joe Hill was tied to a chair. Blindfolded. A small target was pinned to his chest. ‘Let it go, fire,’ he yelled. Rifles protruding from the blacksmith shop at Utah’s state prison obliged. Three of the bullets pierced his heart. The fourth went a little wide.”

In 1951, a firing squad execution in Utah went awry when the state put Eliseo J. Mares to death. He had been sentenced for the 1946 murder of an Ohio sailor who was killed while traveling to California for his marriage. Two of the four bullets missed Mares’s heart. They hit his hip and abdomen. He did not die quickly.

In January 1977, Utah also killed Gary Gilmore by firing squad. Utah law allowed prisoners to choose hanging or firing squad as execution methods. Gilmore elected the latter, saying it would allow him to “die with dignity.”
Gilmore was the first person executed in the U.S. after the Supreme Court‘s 1976 ruling that the death penalty was not a cruel and unusual punishment.

As Time magazine reported, “His neck, waist, wrists and feet were loosely bound to the chair. Twenty-six feet away hung a sailcloth partition with five slits. Hidden behind the curtain stood five riflemen armed with .30-.30 deer rifles, four loaded with steel-jacketed shells, the fifth with a blank.”
Gilmore’s last words: “Let’s do it.”
Is the firing squad humane?
I believe the firing squad has not played a large role in America’s death penalty history because it’s offensive to this country’s evolving standards of decency.

As an anesthesiologist told The Associated Press in March 2023, “Inmates could remain conscious for up to 10 seconds after being shot depending on where bullets strike … and those seconds could be ‘severely painful, especially related to shattering of bone and damage to the spinal cord.’”
States abandoned the firing squad because it was thought to mimic the violence to which executions were responding.

But Hasan’s execution comes at a time of revived interest in firing squads as an execution method, aided by continuing problems with lethal injection. They are now legal in five states: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah.
Idaho is the only state that designates the firing squad as its primary execution method. Idaho state Rep. Bruce Skaug has called the method “certain” and “quick.”
Others agree. In a 2017 opinion, Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote, “In addition to being near instant, death by shooting may also be comparatively painless.”

And in October 2026, former federal appellate judge Alex Kozinski applauded Hegseth’s decision to execute Hasan by firing squad. He was reiterating a view he expressed in a 2014 dissenting opinion: “Eight or ten large-caliber rifle bullets fired at close range can inflict massive damage, causing instant death every time.”

“Sure,” Kozinski added, “firing squads can be messy, but if we are willing to carry out executions, we should not shield ourselves from the reality that we are shedding human blood. If we, as a society, cannot stomach the splatter from an execution carried out by firing squad, then we shouldn’t be carrying out executions at all.”
On Dec. 3, Americans will again have a chance to consider whether they can stomach an execution by firing squad or whether they should be carrying out executions at all.

articles.title: The surge of women elected in the 2026 midterms, particularly women of color, will shape political engagement for a generation of young people
articles.author: David Campbell, Packey J. Dee Professor of American Democracy, University of Notre Dame
paras: On the day after the 2026 midterms, Atlanta’s WSB-TV led off its coverage by showing a series of almost entirely white men get replaced, one by one, by Black women.

Not only had Georgia elected Keisha Lance Bottoms as the nation’s first Black woman governor, African American women had also won positions as secretary of state, attorney general, state school superintendent, agriculture commissioner, insurance commissioner and labor commissioner.

In the legislative branch, Georgia’s likely incoming speaker of the House of Representatives is also a Black woman. Reporter Candace McEwen, herself a Black woman, ended her report by recounting how her 9-year-old goddaughter, upon seeing the graphic showing all the new Black women leaders in Georgia, commented, “I might have a shot!”
As McEwen concluded: “Indeed she does.”

As political scientists who have long studied the effects of women politicians, our research has shown that both McEwen and her young goddaughter are right: When young people see politicians who look like them, they are inspired to be politically engaged.
‘Inspiration now, participation later’
Following the 2026 midterm elections, a record number of women will serve in state and national offices. More women of color will serve in prominent political offices than ever before.

As of this writing — with some races yet to be called — at least 162 women will serve in the U.S. Congress, 138 of them in the House of Representatives, according to the Center for American Women and Politics.

A minimum of 18 women will serve as governors, while 108 will serve in other statewide executive offices. The new Congress will seat an unprecedented 31 Black, 29 Hispanic, nine Asian American/Pacific Islander and four Native American women, and three women of Middle Eastern heritage.

These women of color will no doubt have significant effects on public policy as they draw on their life experiences while governing. In addition, our research shows that they will have another kind of impact on young people in their states and districts. Specifically, when women run for office, they motivate young girls to get involved in politics.

Women of color, however, are especially inspiring for young girls. Not surprisingly, they serve as role models for young girls of color, igniting their political interest and even leading them to envision themselves as running for office one day.

But their impact also extends to white girls, who are inspired by seeing these women overcome the double barriers of gender and race. This inspiration while young leads to greater political participation in adulthood.
There’s the concrete connection: Inspiration now, participation later.
‘You can’t be what you can’t see’

While teenagers typically do not spend a lot of time following politics, they often absorb lessons from their political environment by osmosis, such as a news story shared on social media, passing by a billboard or holding a conversation with a parent or teacher. Because politics has historically been a man’s game – and a white man’s game at that – seeing women, and women of color especially, in public life changes their default assumption about who is suited to govern.

Politics is no longer just for white men. In the famous words of civil and children’s rights advocate Marian Wright Edelman, you can’t be what you can’t see. When young women see women in positions of leadership, they believe they can be leaders too.
If we left the story here, the election of all these women of color may seem like an unmitigated win for the long-term vitality of American democracy. But the story is a little more complicated.
The historic wave of women is a win for the future of the Democrats specifically. This is because the overwhelming majority of these newly elected women are Democrats.
‘Stunning party imbalance’
Of the 162 women who have officially won their midterm House or Senate races so far, 122 – 75% – of them are Democrats. That’s a stunning party imbalance.

There is an even greater imbalance for women of color. In Georgia, all the African American women elected to statewide office are Democrats. In the U.S. House, all but four of the women of color are Democrats; in the Senate, it’s 100%.
This matters because we have also found that young people are most likely to see candidates from their own party as role models.

Lest you doubt that we can speak of teenagers as Democrats or Republicans, study after study finds that party attachments develop young, and the same polarization found among adults is mirrored in their children.

In other words, the girls who are inspired by this wave of women are far more likely to be Democrats than Republicans. Since partisan teens usually grow up to be partisan adults, this suggests that future Democratic women – whether they be racial minorities or whites – will be more politically engaged in adulthood.

For all the attention paid to the political choices of young Republican men, the party should be worried about the future of Republican women. Without more women politicians representing the GOP, Republican girls are likely to continue seeing politics as a man’s game and stay on the sidelines of civic life.
This doesn’t mean this wave of mostly Democratic women politicians won’t have any impact on Republican teens.
When women of either party run for office, both Republican girls and boys change their attitudes about women.

In general, Republican teens are less likely than Democrats to think that women have the necessary traits to be political leaders. But when they live in a community where women candidates run, they come to see women as fit to govern.
Why the change among Republicans and not Democrats? To be blunt, it is because Democratic kids do not need to be convinced that women are as capable of leadership as men.
Representation matters. We have found that barrier-breakers and firsts are particularly effective in changing young people’s beliefs and behaviors. The 2026 midterm elections produced many of those.
We expect that the effects will play out for years to come as more women believe that in politics, they have a shot.

articles.title: Backlash against data centers helped Democrats win the midterms
articles.author: Jesse Usher Barrett, Graduate Poll Fellow in Political Science, UMass Amherst
paras: The 2026 midterm elections that swept Democrats into power in Congress and state legislatures also delivered a stunning rebuke to the artificial intelligence industry.

Ballot measures that limited the construction of data centers – from California to Kansas to North Dakota – were approved by voters in 40 of 41 instances. These measures included the Kansas prohibition on construction of a type of battery energy storage system, a 180-day moratorium on data centers in Maine, and the outright ban on data center construction in Ohio.

Drawing on recent survey data, we suggest that the Democratic sweep and the nationwide rejection of data centers are related. Republicans’ connections with an unpopular AI industry may have contributed to their poor showing at the polls.
We are survey researchers. Our August 2026 survey of a nationally representative sample of 1,000 American adults shows that opposition to data centers is widespread.

The survey shows that 65% of Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their communities. This opposition is bipartisan, with 76% of Democrats, 67% of independents and 52% of Republicans opposed to the sites.

To better understand the sources of this opposition, we asked respondents to explain it in their own words. Twenty-eight percent of respondents voiced concerns about the negative environmental impact of data centers. One respondent stated: “Draining our water reserves significantly with a data center would be catastrophic to our region.”

Some respondents, 15%, also expressed concerns about data centers’ negative impact on their quality of life. For example, one respondent said: “Noise issues, energy issues and visual site are three issues that are major concerns for a AI data center to be in the area I live in.”

Ten percent of respondents singled out the centers’ connection to increased utility costs. One respondent said that “ever since a data center has been built in my local area the prices of water and electricity have more than doubled.”

Finally, 13% of respondents expressed a broad distrust of AI and the industry itself, with one stating, “I think that AI needs to be better regulated and a lot more developed and proven safe before any massive full scale deployment.”

Despite mounting public opposition to data centers, President Donald Trump expressed strong support for data center construction before Election Day. He said that if Americans want to live in “crime-infested areas” and “squalor,” they should not have a data center. Days after the midterms, Trump threatened to penalize U.S. companies that build data centers overseas.

As widespread opposition to data centers grew through 2026, Republican congressional candidates increasingly had to weigh loyalty to Trump against local backlash. As Election Day neared, many Republican candidates had distanced themselves from unrestricted data center construction.
In contrast, many Democrats made opposition to data centers an important theme of their campaigns.
Our poll suggests that these efforts may have resonated with voters.

Among Americans who expressed opposition to data centers, 48% indicated they would support the local Democratic candidate in the U.S. House of Representatives, compared to 25% for the Republican candidate. And 47% of those living in states that held a Senate election were planning on voting for the Democratic candidate, while 28% planned to vote for the Republican Senate candidate.
Even taking partisanship, ideology and demographic characteristics into account, opposition to data centers was associated with an intention to support Democratic House and Senate candidates.

Given widespread public concern about data center construction, Democrats have electoral incentives to make AI regulation a part of their legislative agenda in the new Congress. Whether or not they enact new legislation, popular opposition to data centers is unlikely to abate anytime soon.

articles.title: Joanne Young waived her anonymity – my research shows why survivors of sexual violence make this brave choice
articles.author: Orla Muldoon, Professor of Psychology, University of Limerick, and Head of School of Psychology, Queens Belfast, Queen's University Belfast
paras: Echoing the case of Gisèle Pelicot in France, Joanne Young waived her right to anonymity following the conviction of her ex-husband for drugging her, raping her and allowing other men to rape her too. Philip Young had routinely drugged his wife over many years, soliciting men online to come into their home and rape her.
In the UK and Ireland, victims of sexual violence are entitled to lifelong anonymity. This reflects an enduring reality: rape and sexual assault remain highly stigmatising experiences.

Yet there is growing evidence that survivors are choosing to forgo that protection. Along with colleagues, I have been systematically studying those who choose to waive their right to anonymity. Though survivors’ experiences are very different, common themes emerge.
By waiving this right, Young and Pelicot have opened up a conversation about violence against women and girls. This conversation is sorely needed.

During their trial, Norman Macksoni, Richard Wilkins, Connor Sanderson-Doyle and Mohammed Hassan argued that their sexual activity with the unconscious Joanne Young was consensual as her then-husband gave consent. Another man, Dean Hamilton, admitted charges including rape in February, and Philip Young also pleaded guilty at an earlier hearing to a string of offences.

Pelicot and supporters of Young have said that shame must change sides. They are not wrong. In the UK case, here is a cohort of men who argued in open court that a husband has the power to decide who has sexual access to his wife. That is both shocking and shameful.

Victims of sexual assault experience domination of their bodily autonomy in the most intimate way. And they often describe their experiences in court as similarly intrusive and violating. Intimate videos are replayed, there can be extensive scrutiny of their sexual history and relentless questions about their consent.

Reasserting their agency is another key motivation of those who waive their anonymity. Speaking can be empowering after a trial where they have had very little control over the outcome. In the all too rare instances when a conviction is secured (unlike when it is not), victims are free to speak. Those who feel they have survived both the abuse and the judicial system often feel compelled to speak on behalf of the many others who don’t seek or get justice.

There is a final reason that survivors can be motivated to waive their anonymity. Doing so can allow them to find solidarity with others who share their experience. Sexual violence is associated with a high burden of ill health compared to other traumatic life events. This might be mental health consequences including depression and post-traumatic stress, and physical issues including cardiovascular, metabolic and immune disorders.

Research consistently shows that deliberate, intentional acts of violence disproportionately damage people’s faith in others. This can make it difficult for victims to connect with others. This is amplified in cases where the perpetrator is a family member. Previously trusted husbands and fathers have not only exploited their position in the family unit, they have fractured relationships.

For many, and particularly for women where family roles are heavily emphasised, much of their identity is defined by these relationships: daughter, wife or mother. Alongside shame, sexual abuse corrupts these identity-based relationships, further disconnecting victims when they need support.

Philip Young, a former Conservative councillor in Swindon, Wiltshire, harnessed the power of like-minded others. At short notice, after he had drugged Joanne, he was able to find ample men in a small geographical area willing to assault his unconscious wife.
In going public, Young and Pelicot have both harnessed the power of like-minded others for good. Waiving anonymity can allow victims to connect with others at a very vulnerable point in their lives.

But Lavinia Kerwick, the first woman in Ireland to waive her anonymity after the conviction of her rapist in 1991, has described the burden of doing so. The survivor rather than the perpetrator becomes publicly synonymous with the crime. It can become a lens through which others see victims.

Waiving anonymity is not for everyone and certainly shouldn’t be an expectation placed on survivors. And clearly survivors make their decisions based on their own circumstances and concerns. Either way, it is a difficult decision.

Survivors are acutely aware that waiving anonymity comes at a personal cost. But for those who do, their actions are driven by collective rather than personal concerns. In research with colleagues, we have referred to this phenomenon as collective post-traumatic growth. After their trauma, survivors rebuild a view of the world that includes the need for a different future, a better one for all. Drawing strength from the support and solidarity after their disclosure, they are driven to act on behalf of others.

Sexual violence is not simply a private, personal matter. It is a corrosive social force, the effects of which extend far beyond the family home. It damages relationships and communities, and shatters the integrity of our social, judicial and political institutions. Young, Pelicot and others waive their anonymity to progress social, political and legislative change for everyone. It’s time to trade in the shame and offer them our gratitude.
Orla Muldoon has received funding from the European Research Council.

articles.title: The University of Florida revives the ‘Gator bait’ cheer, reversing a ban over its troubling history
articles.author: Mark V. Barrow, Jr., Professor of History, Virginia Tech
paras: The sold-out crowd at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium, better known as “The Swamp,” roared with excitement as the University of Florida revived its “Gator bait” cheer at its 2026 season opener.

When the marching band played the familiar cue, thousands of fans responded with the “Gator chomp,” raising their outstretched arms and repeatedly opening and closing their hands like alligator jaws while shouting “Gator bait!”

The decision to bring back the popular cheer reversed a ban imposed in 2020 by University of Florida President Kent Fuchs, who was concerned about its racist origins amid the nationwide reckoning over race that followed the murder of George Floyd.

Current university president Stuart Bell remarked in an interview prior to his official appointment that “traditions matter” and suggested that the cheer could return because it remained “meaningful to the Gator family.” Since then, the university has restored the cheer, though it has not publicly identified who formally authorized its return.

The controversy surrounding this chant has often been framed narrowly by its supporters as a dispute over tradition versus political correctness. However, it raises important questions about whether a public university should continue to embrace a tradition that risks making some students and alumni feel less welcome on campus.

As an environmental and cultural historian and author of “Gator!: The Making of America’s Iconic Reptile, from First Encounters to Florida Man,” I’ve spent years researching how alligators became intertwined with ideas about race, nature and Southern identity. My research points to a deeper history largely absent from the public debate over the cheer.
The making of ‘alligator bait’ as a racial slur

The roots of the “alligator bait” trope stretch back to the 18th century, when French explorers in North America claimed that a “certain exhalation” given off from Black skin attracted the voracious reptiles.
White plantation owners eagerly took up this racist theory because it discouraged enslaved people from fleeing into Southern swamps and marshes, where pursuing runaways was often difficult.

After the Civil War, as formerly enslaved people sought economic, educational and political advancement, many white Americans responded with efforts to reassert white supremacy. Alongside disenfranchisement, Jim Crow segregation and racial terrorism, they promoted stereotypes that demeaned and dehumanized African Americans.

One of these racist stereotypes was the depiction of Black Americans, especially children, as natural prey for alligators. Though it operated through images and ideas rather than physical force, the stereotype reinforced beliefs in Black inferiority. It also helped justify the intimidation, exclusion and violence that African Americans routinely faced during this period.

It was in this context that the racial slur “alligator bait” began circulating widely in the late 19th century. A bestselling photograph bearing that title, published in 1897, helped popularize the slur. Although the composite image of nine naked African American toddlers did not include an actual alligator, its title invited viewers to imagine Black children as special targets of the reptile.

The epithet soon spread through newspapers, postcards, editorial cartoons, songs and films. Ostensibly humorous images of alligators threatening or consuming Black Americans, especially children, also circulated widely across the U.S.

Whether Black children were ever actually used as bait to hunt alligators remains a subject of historical debate. But what is beyond dispute is that these images helped entrench degrading associations between African Americans and alligators in American popular culture for decades.
‘Gator bait’ comes to campus

As the phrase alligator bait gained currency across the United States, it also began appearing in a new setting: University of Florida football games. The earliest published reference to the cheer seems to be a 1939 newspaper account of a home game against Georgia Tech.

When Georgia Tech’s Yellow Jackets took the field, Florida students taunted the all-white team with cries of “alligator bait.” Georgia Tech’s coach used the insult to motivate his players, asking whether they could imagine “anything lower than that.”

While it is impossible to know precisely how everyone present understood the phrase, it entered Florida football culture at a time when “alligator bait” remained a recognizable racial slur. By the late 1940s, the shortened form, “Gator bait,” which was both easier to chant and more closely aligned with the university’s “Gators” nickname, had become a regular fixture at Florida football games.

The cheer remained firmly embedded in campus culture as the university navigated the slow and often contentious process of desegregation. Like most Southern universities, the University of Florida resisted admitting Black students, enrolling its first African American law student, George H. Starke, only after a court order in 1958. The first Black undergraduates arrived four years later, and the football team remained segregated until 1968.

Desegregation did not immediately transform the broader campus culture. The university continued to embrace traditions that celebrated the Confederacy and romanticized the Old South. In 1962, football coach Ray Graves placed decals of the Confederate battle flag on his players’ helmets before the Gator Bowl.

As late as the 1970s, the all-white Kappa Alpha fraternity continued a decades-long tradition of staging an annual “Old South” weekend that featured students parading in Confederate uniforms. In the 1950s and 1960s, that celebration even included a mock execution of Union General William T. Sherman and a secession proclamation.

When the student newspaper surveyed the campus in 1968 about whether to continue playing “Dixie” – the unofficial anthem of the Confederate States of America – at football games, 83% of students supported the practice. But the majority of Black students surveyed opposed it. “Dixie” remained a game-day staple until 1973.
The many meanings of ‘Gator bait’

By the late 20th century, most Florida fans no longer understood “Gator bait” through the lens of Jim Crow-era racial stereotypes. Decades of use at football games had transformed the chant into a symbol of school spirit and athletic success.

No individual played a larger role in that transformation than Lawrence Wright, the hard-hitting safety who helped lead Florida to its first national championship. Wright, who is African American, did not invent the cheer, as is often claimed, but he helped elevate it to iconic status. Following Florida’s victory over rival Florida State in 1995, he famously rallied fans with the refrain, “If you ain’t a Gator, you must be Gator bait.”

When the Gators became national champions the next season, the chant became even more deeply enshrined in Florida football culture. For most fans, “Gator bait” came to symbolize pride in the university rather than anything connected to the phrase’s earlier racist history.
History clashes with the present
Yet that history never disappeared.
While most fans were unaware of it, “alligator bait” remained a documented racial slur, creating a tension between the phrase’s historical origins and its modern meaning.

That tension came to a head in 2020, when Fuchs suspended the cheer amid a broader university effort to address racism and inequity. While acknowledging that he knew of “no evidence of racism associated with our ‘Gator Bait’ cheer at UF sporting events,” Fuchs argued that the phrase’s “horrific historic racist imagery” warranted its retirement.

Critics, including Wright, responded that the cheer’s meaning at Florida had become detached from those historical associations. “Gator bait” was a cherished university tradition, they argued, neither generally understood nor intended as racist.
Six years later, under Bell, the university has reinstated the cheer amid a political and cultural climate markedly different from the one that had prompted its suspension.

Still, I believe the debate surrounding its return reveals that the controversy has never simply been about political correctness or school spirit. In my view, it is also about how institutions reckon with difficult histories and whether traditions can be separated from the historical meanings that gave rise to them.
Even if most fans today understand the cheer as an expression of school spirit, universities do not simply inherit traditions. They choose which ones they wish to preserve, modify or discard.

Whether the university made the right decision is open to debate. What is not in dispute is that the “Gator bait” cheer emerged during a period when “alligator bait” functioned as a racial slur and the University of Florida excluded Black students while embracing traditions that celebrated the Confederacy.
The Conversation reached out to the university, and it declined to add to Bell’s previous comments on this matter.
The University of Florida is a founding partner of The Conversation.
Mark V. Barrow, Jr. earned his BA in History at the University of Florida in 1985 and has received funding from the National Endowment for the Humanities.

articles.title: Be Ready stockpiling advice is missing something vital. You can fix it, today
articles.author: James David Raven, Doctoral researcher, Anglia Ruskin University
paras: Just hours after the UK government launched its Be Ready campaign in October, Storm Austen struck, shortly followed by Storm Boelo. Winds exceeded 80mph, causing power cuts that affected around 838,000 people, some for days.
Less than a month later, on November 12, a major Microsoft outage disrupted access to Outlook and other services for almost 24 hours, leaving hospitals, schools and workplaces in disarray.

In today’s complex world, we can rarely pinpoint the timing, impact or form of a disruption. It can happen without warning, making initiatives like Be Ready – which advises households to keep a three-day supply of food and drink in case of emergencies – a necessity.

But the Be Ready guide is, in effect, little more than a shopping list. It does not mention behaviour or actions, and is missing something just as important as stockpiled tins and bottles: a firm, agreed plan.

My research focuses on preparation for the “inevitable but opaque” disruption that we have seen in the last few months. We know that there will be disruption, but not when, what form it will take, or how bad it will be.

When families visit a busy theme park or festival, they often agree a rule like “if we get separated, meet at the entrance”. Few realise this kind of accepted information has a name: common knowledge.
When everyone hears the rule together, each person knows the others also know it. Nobody wonders whether the others will turn up, and nobody is left guessing.

A blackout is like getting lost in a theme park, except there’s no tannoy and no phone. With a quick text or call off the table, the rule must be in place before you need it. We therefore need to stockpile common knowledge, just as we stockpile water, food and medicine.

In the late 1950s, American economist Thomas Schelling asked people where and when they would meet someone in New York City with no way to communicate. Many picked noon at the information booth in Grand Central Station, showing that guessing can work when one place stands out.

For households, the problem is the opposite: they have too many obvious options. On any given day, a family may be split across work, school and home. What seems obvious to one person may not be obvious to another.

If disaster strikes, one person might wait at the office while another stays put at home. Both might then go out looking for each other. Without common knowledge, neither has any idea where to go or what to expect.
How to stockpile common knowledge
The good news is that building a stockpile of common knowledge is quick and easy. Here are four key points your plan should take into consideration:

Meeting place and time: Home is the obvious first choice, but you need a fallback location if it could become unsafe (due to flood risk, for example). This should be somewhere walkable and less reliant on power, such as a community building. It is crucial to set a time rule. If by an agreed time you haven’t met at home, go to the fallback location.

Phone times: If the power fails but the networks stay on, every bit of battery counts. If you need to talk to someone regularly, agree to turn phones on for 10 minutes every three hours. Choose an easy pattern so you can all remember it, even under stress: at midday, 3pm, 6pm and so on.

Pickup plans: Schools will wait for an adult, so decide who will collect children or other dependants. Agree in advance to prevent both of you from turning up, or worse, each assuming the other will go.

Write it down: Most important, agree on these things together long before anything goes wrong. It doesn’t need to be a formal crisis-style talk – doing it over dinner, for example, can make it less alarming for children. Once agreed, write your common knowledge down on card, not a phone or laptop. Keep copies in key places such as school bags, briefcases, on the fridge and in the car’s glove compartment.
While tinned food and bottled water are essential in a crisis, common knowledge is what makes any plan work when stress and confusion are likely to peak.

Versions of this already exist: Scotland’s advice, for instance, already includes meeting places, but neither it nor the UK’s checklist explains why agreeing together matters, or covers phone-on times and a time rule.
There is also not not a one-size-fits-all solution. Some households will find this harder than others, but the underlying principle can be adapted.

My plea is therefore a simple one. Sit down with your family this week, and agree your plan. Follow the government’s stockpiling advice, of course, but add one thing to your checklist: a plan that everyone already knows.

articles.title: What does the UK-EU ‘reset’ deal mean for immigration and tuition fees?
articles.author: Alan Manning, Professor of Economics, London School of Economics and Political Science
paras: Much of the UK-EU “reset” talks, held in Brussels on November 20, were on the issue of migration. The newly announced measures largely centre on young people and students, with deals hinging on an EU demand to reduce tuition fees for EU students at UK universities. The newly struck deals also mention irregular migration, including channel crossings.

The biggest questions – a return to free movement, the single market or the customs union – are still off the table, but the talks mark a closer post-Brexit relationship between the UK and the EU on migration. So where are we likely to see changes?

First and foremost is the Youth Experience Scheme (YES), which will allow up to 100,000 young people a year to migrate between the UK and EU to work or study for up to three years. The scheme will not be rolled out immediately, and is expected to take effect between 2028 and 2030.
In practice, this will probably be similar to the UK’s current agreements with some non-EU countries, including New Zealand and Canada.

The UK’s schemes with these other countries only use around 25% of their capped numbers, but the cap on the EU scheme will likely be met. This will, of course, raise EU immigration into the UK. But it does not mean 100,000 new arrivals – some coming on the new scheme could previously have come via other channels.
The scheme will also raise UK emigration to EU countries, as some young British people will use the scheme to go to work in the EU. This will limit the overall effect on net migration.
Under the new rules, youth mobility could reach something close to an equilibrium, with a comparable number entering and exiting every year. The impact on net migration could therefore be very small.

The issue of university tuition fees proved to be a sticking point in the negotiations. The EU wants UK and EU students to both pay the same fees as home students – currently £9,790 per year in the UK. A six-month period has been given for these negotiations to be finalised.

The UK may be reluctant because lower tuition fees for EU citizens would prove unpopular among UK universities. While universities widely criticised the rise in EU student fees immediately after the Brexit vote, they have now come to depend on the extra cash.

In July 2026, Vivienne Stern, the CEO of Universities UK, an industry body for UK universities, stated that giving EU students home fee status would now worsen the financial situation for UK universities.

During the Brexit campaign, the “Vote Leave, take back control” slogan promised more control over borders. The Leave campaign argued that EU free movement gave the UK no say over how many EU migrants arrived.

But an irony of Brexit is that it gave the UK less control over asylum claims, including those of people crossing the English Channel in small boats. This was largely because Brexit made UK-EU cooperation harder.
Asylum claims rose from about 40,000 a year pre-pandemic to 100,000 afterwards. In 2019, 1,800 people reach the UK via small boat crossings. The number rose to over 45,000 in 2022.

Although Channel crossings would likely have risen even if the UK had stayed in the EU, Brexit probably reduced control over irregular migration and asylum claims. After Brexit, the UK lost access to the Dublin convention on returns, and with it, the Eurodac asylum database.
This meant cooperation with European countries was no longer automatic, and made the UK a de facto appeals court for asylum-seekers whose EU claims had failed.

Eurodac allows authorities to check asylum seekers’ previous claims and criminal records, and to identify those who had previously applied within the EU. UK authorities have stated that they would like to regain access to Eurodac.

The summit’s joint statement specifically mentions the EU’s Channel Action Plan to tackle dangerous crossings of the English Channel, which the UK joined in July 2026. There were also commitments to a “Structured Dialogue on migration”. All of this is in keeping with the UK government’s efforts to “restore order and control to our borders”.

But this aspect of migration – by far the most politicised among the British electorate – will be the hardest to rein in. Access to Eurodac is complicated, and cannot be solved with one quick summit. Brexit may therefore leave the UK with reduced control over the area of migration where voters want it most.
Alan Manning receives funding from ESRC through the Centre for Economic Performance at LSE. He is a member of the Labour Party

articles.title: Burnham in Brussels: why party politics still defines the UK’s relationship with Europe
articles.author: Martin Steven, Senior Lecturer, School of Global Affairs, Lancaster University
paras: Andy Burnham has attended his first EU-UK summit in Brussels with major agreements reached on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions. Ultimately though, the prime minister will have understood that this was merely the start of new political negotiations. Back home in the UK, he has started a “national conversation” on the future of UK-EU relations that gained momentum rapidly.

Burnham held talks with European Council president Antonio Costa and president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen. Both Burnham and Costa come from sister social democratic parties and both are former mayors – Burnham of Greater Manchester and Costa of Lisbon. This could make for smoother meetings in future than in the months and years after the 2016 Brexit referendum.

In the run up to the talks, the prime minister had repeatedly claimed that the Conservatives failed to get a good deal from the EU. As part of former prime minister Keir Starmer’s “reset” of relations with Europe, then-business secretary, Peter Kyle, and European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera signed a deal committing the UK and the EU to closer cooperation on trade.

Like Costa and Burnham, Ribera is also from a European social democratic party (the Spanish Socialist Workers Party, or PSOE). Senior figures in Labour have long admired the electoral success of social democrats in both Spain and Portugal.

When it comes to claims of the UK having had a bad deal, there is one explanation that is under-discussed. It has its roots in the internal party politics of the centre-right in Europe. Ahead of the 2009 European Parliament elections, the then-Conservative leader David Cameron decided to leave the European People’s Party (a bloc of centre-right pro-European parties).

Cameron went on to set up a new right-of-centre eurosceptic faction with parties from Poland and the Czech Republic. But he underestimated how hurt highly influential EU figures like German chancellor Angela Merkel were by the move. So when it came to negotiating a better deal with the EU ahead of the 2016 referendum, Merkel and other figures had not forgotten Cameron’s betrayal. As such, they felt disinclined to meet him half way.
Burnham is walking a fine line

Youth mobility, migration, food exports and emissions are all important issues. But the broader discussion is increasingly about the politics around Brexit rather than the rights and wrongs of Brexit itself.

The UK is not going to rejoin the EU in the near future. Burnham even said when standing in the Makerfield byelection that first and foremost he wants to sort the consequences of Brexit rather than necessarily the outcome.

Now Burnham is increasingly focused on the claim that Brexit hasn’t worked for British voters – without saying it was completely wrong. He may understand that aiming to reverse Brexit in a binary way could simply open up new problems. It could even finish his premiership in the same way that it ended the tenures of multiple prime ministers before him.

In contrast, however, Burnham understands that he has the political capital to discuss the downsides of Brexit. For now, at least, he can do this in a way that is unlikely to result in much political damage to his government. While not completely without risk, he has calculated that the benefits of discussing Brexit outweigh any costs.

These costs could include the fragile “red wall” of Labour seats in northern England and the Midlands. The party knows all too well that this could flip to Reform UK the next time the country goes to the polls.

But those voters who have already moved to Reform are something of a sunk cost for Labour. For now, it seems Burnham sees more advantages in drawing voters away from the Liberal Democrats and the Greens than he sees disadvantages in alienating supporters of Reform. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch appears to be sensitive to the fact that many people disapprove of how the Tories handled Brexit – whether they voted Remain or Leave.
At the height of the Brexit chaos, however, Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester and so can revisit the issue in a fresh way, untainted by the Westminister turbulence of that time.

His predecessor Starmer was frequently seen as being paralysed by caution. Burnham appears to know how to talk about difficult issues lightly and fluently – his own parliamentary seat overwhelmingly voted Leave in 2016.

He may or may not truly want to see the UK rejoin the EU at some point – he has sometimes sent out mixed signals on the issue. But he certainly has the firm aim of removing the toxicity from the issue and having a “national conversation”. To do this, the prime minister will have to consider how Westminster relates to Brussels as well as how it relates to constituencies like his own in Makerfield.

Martin Steven does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Independent, Gen Z and Latino voters helped deliver a Democratic wave in 2026 – but that doesn’t mean a lasting realignment
articles.author: Thom Reilly, Professor and Co-Director of the Center for an Independent and Sustainable Democracy; School of Public Affairs, Arizona State University
paras: The Democratic wave in the 2026 midterm elections raises an important question about American politics. Are independent, Gen Z and Latino voters building a new Democratic coalition, or are they sending a warning to both parties that their support cannot be taken for granted?
The preliminary evidence suggests something more complicated.

Our analysis, including a deep dive into the 2026 Voter Poll conducted by the market research firm SSRS, points to three factors behind the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories: a substantial shift among independent voters toward Democratic candidates, stronger Democratic turnout relative to Republicans, and declining enthusiasm among voters who supported Donald Trump in 2024.
Gen Z, who are people born from 1997 to 2012, and Latino voters played important roles in these shifts.

But the results should not automatically be interpreted as a lasting Democratic realignment. These voters may be demonstrating a willingness to reconsider their political choices when governing parties fail to meet their expectations.

The overlapping influence of independent, younger and Latino voters helps explain the scale of the Democratic gains. Our analysis, based on voter poll data, suggests that independents, who made up about one-third of voters, contributed approximately 52% of the Democrats’ national popular vote margin in House races. Latino voters contributed an estimated 23% of that margin, while voters ages 18 to 29 contributed approximately 39%.
Because these groups overlap, their contributions cannot be added together. But the figures illustrate how important each was to the Democratic advantage.
In our book, “The Independent Voter,” co-authored with Omar Ali, we examine the growing influence of independent voters and their often unpredictable voting behavior.
Independents helped determine the outcome
Independent voters, among the most important contributors to Democratic victories in the 2026 midterms, have repeatedly demonstrated a willingness to shift between parties.

In 2008, they favored Democratic presidential candidate Barack Obama by 8 percentage points. Four years later, they backed Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney by 5 points. In the 2016 presidential election, independents favored Republican Trump by 4 points before swinging toward Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, supporting him by 13 points.

In the 2024 presidential election, independents narrowly favored Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump, 49% to 46%. However, Trump performed better among independents in key battleground states, including Arizona, Georgia, Pennsylvania and North Carolina.
In our research spanning nearly five decades, Dan Hunting and I, Thom Reilly, found that independents exhibit considerably greater volatility in their voting patterns than Democrats and Republicans.

The 3-point advantage independents gave Harris in 2024 provides a useful baseline for understanding their much larger shift toward Democratic candidates in 2026. A November 2026 national survey of more than 90,000 people found that voters identifying with neither major party favored Democratic House candidates by more than 20 percentage points.

Our analysis of voter poll data showed that independents favored House Democrats by 59% to 37%. In addition, independents’ support was consequential in several Republican-held Senate seats that flipped to Democrats, with independent voters providing the margin needed for victory in six of the nine races: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Mississippi, Ohio and South Carolina.

The emerging pattern may represent another turn in a longer cycle of electoral volatility among independents. Rather than embracing either party, independent voters appear willing to reconsider their choices as political and economic conditions change.
Did Republicans switch sides or stay home?
There is some disagreement about what produced the midterm Democratic wave.

Brookings scholars Elaine Kamarck and William Galston argue that Republican abstention – those who chose not to vote – was more important nationally than large-scale partisan crossover voting. They report that only approximately 6% of self-identified Republicans voted for Democratic House candidates.
Yet the evidence also demonstrates some crossover voting.
An analysis by the research firm NORC found that approximately 1 in 10 2024 Trump voters in 2026 supported Democratic Senate candidates in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina and Texas.
Both dynamics appear to have played a role.

Democrats benefited from stronger participation among their supporters and reduced turnout among some voters who backed Trump in 2024. In several competitive races, Republican defections and strong independent support also contributed to Democratic victories.

Understanding these differences is important. A shift in election results does not necessarily mean voters have changed their party loyalties. It may reflect changes in who participates. The 2026 results suggest that both factors were at work.
Younger voters shifted sharply toward Democrats
Gen Z voters were another important part of the Democratic gains.

In 2026, 66% of voters ages 18–29 supported Democratic House candidates, compared with 30% who backed Republicans. That 36-point Democratic advantage was substantially larger than the 14-point margin in 2024, according to Tufts University.

There was also evidence of voters switching party choices. Among young people who voted for Trump in 2024 and participated in the 2026 election, 16% supported a Democratic House candidate. And 67% of young voters disapproved of Trump’s performance as president in 2026.
Gallup found that 56% of Gen Z adults identify as political independents, underscoring the weaker ties many younger Americans have to the two major parties.

Combined with economic dissatisfaction and distrust of political institutions, this suggests that younger voters may be especially willing to reconsider their choices when the party in power fails to meet their expectations or deliver on its promises.
Latino voters also shifted substantially
Latino voters showed a similar pattern, but with some differences.
More than 6 in 10 Latino voters supported Democratic House candidates in 2026, according to a NORC survey. That reverses much of the Republican gains among these voters in 2024.

There was also evidence of volatility among Latinos. A postelection survey by UnidosUS and BSP Research found that 17% of Latino voters who supported Trump in 2024 voted for Democratic House candidates in 2026, compared with just 3% of Harris voters who supported Republicans.
Texas offers an example of how these voting groups overlapped.

According to our analysis of the voter poll data, 68% of Latino voters supported Democrat James Talarico, compared with 30% who backed his Republican opponent. Among voters ages 18 to 29, Talarico won 79% to 19%, while independents favored him by 64% to 33%.
Of course, these groups overlap. A voter can be Latino, young and independent, so their contributions cannot simply be added together numerically.
Still, Latinos’ strong support for Talarico illustrates how shifts among these voting groups helped Democrats win in a traditionally Republican state, perhaps shaping a new composite demographic.
A warning for both political parties
The lesson of 2026 may be less about Democratic realignment than about political accountability.
Republicans benefited in 2024 from dissatisfaction with Democratic governance. Two years later, Democrats benefited from dissatisfaction with Republican governance.
Yet the scale of the Democratic victories should not be understated.

Widespread dissatisfaction with Trump’s presidency – his handling of the economy, the war in Iran, harsh immigration enforcement policies and concerns about corruption – contributed to a sweeping rejection of his administration and Republican leadership at both the federal and state levels. That includes a Congress that many voters believed had failed to hold him accountable.
Even so, neither party should assume that independents, younger voters or Latinos now belong to its camp.

America’s founders recognized the dangers of excessive party loyalty. In his 1796 farewell address, George Washington warned about the divisive influence of political parties and the dangers of placing party allegiance above the public interest.
More than two centuries later, the growing influence of voters with weaker ties to the major parties raises a similar question about the role of political parties in American democracy.
The 2026 election may not signal a lasting political realignment. Instead, it may reflect an electorate increasingly willing to hold both parties accountable.
For Democrats and Republicans alike, winning an election does not necessarily mean winning voters’ lasting loyalty.

articles.title: Diplomacy, humour and avoidance – what we found when we investigated friendships across class divides
articles.author: Sam Friedman, Professor of Sociology, Department of Sociology, London School of Economics and Political Science
paras: Several years ago, the US economist Raj Chetty and his team at Harvard University analysed billions of ties on Facebook in a bid to learn more about social mobility. Their findings highlighted an important link between cross-class friendship and social mobility. Specifically, they found that people from low-income backgrounds who have more friends from wealthier backgrounds tend to have better chances of earning more as adults.

The paper was published in the journal Nature in 2022. Last year, a report from the Behavioural Insights Team came to the same conclusions in the UK. Both have since been seized upon by policymakers seeking to boost social mobility in the general population.

But we were puzzled. Not only did this work seem to rely on a speculative understanding of how friendships actually work, but the conclusions fly in the face of decades of sociological research. Specifically, that friendship rests on reciprocity between friends, not one-way transfers.

In our new paper, we investigated this tension via 42 in-depth interviews with people in cross-class friendships in the UK. We found that these friendships can indeed produce “social capital”. That is, more privileged friends often provide financial support or cultural guidance to less privileged friends navigating elite spaces. Yet our research also underlines the limitations of characterising cross-class friendship in this way.

In our interviews, when support tended to flow only one way, it generated feelings of inequality or indebtedness, and often sent friendships into a downward spiral. Take Tania (not her real name), a researcher who was white and from a lower-middle-class background. She met Florence at Durham University, where Tania was struggling with the “social side of things”.

In these alien environments, Florence, who was privately educated, acted as what Tania called her “pathfinder”. Tania watched how Florence worked a room. She wasn’t comfortable doing the same on her own terms, so she mirrored how Florence “took up space”.

Yet Tania had mixed feelings about this. It had helped her navigate a career in the civil service – she became “posh Tania” at work – but she was troubled by the feeling that the friendship felt contingent on her assimilation. In other words, if she “dropped back down”, Florence might not stick around.

Against the arguments of the original study in Nature, the successful cross-class friendships we studied were not based on one-way transfers. Rather, they relied on a careful negotiation of class difference, which we term “class diplomacy”.

Diplomacy is a useful term, because it shows how managing class difference is an ongoing part of these friendships. It requires significant emotion work (although this burden is not necessarily felt equally) and demands certain social skills from both parties.

We identified three modes of class diplomacy: joking, avoiding and confronting. First, many friends used teasing and self-deprecation to voice and defuse class tensions. Humour was present across genders, but it was more overtly connected to class in male friendships. Typically, it played out in terms of mocking oneself or each other in class terms.

Peter, a banker from a white working-class family, explained the enduring role that “taking the piss” played in his friendship with Julian (“your typical private schoolboy jokes”). What was important, though, was that Julian would take this on the chin. In this way, joking – particularly jokes that punched upwards – recognised class difference but also registered how it affected their experiences in different ways.

The second way diplomacy played out was via the choice many had made to avoid discussing class. Avoidance allowed forms of connection to flourish – interviewees told us these would be stymied if they were to confront class.

But at the same time, interviewees were acutely aware of how class difference continually threatened the friendship. Both friends intricately navigated how and when to coordinate their mutual avoidance.

Many described pivoting to other sources of shared connection such as gender, race, sexuality or taste. This did not cancel out tensions – class “landmines” – yet focusing on commonality provided a kind of refuge.

Others chose to confront class difference head-on. These participants, disproportionately women, acknowledged the risks of this honesty, but said that, if accompanied by sensitivity, it could be productive.

Shanthi and Nadia agreed that their different backgrounds had largely been superseded by the “bonding effect” of being two women of colour growing up in a “very white” area. Yet the issue of money was an ongoing tension.

Nadia, whose upbringing had been marked by economic precarity, was uncomfortable with Shanthi continually offering to buy her things. Shanthi realised that even if her offers were coming from a “place of love”, they almost legitimised a power difference.

Class diplomacy paves the way for forms of exchange and reciprocity to flourish between friends. This is vital for friendships across class to persist. In the relationships we studied, this also had a mutually socialising effect that often led to a heightened sensitivity to class inequality.

Friends spoke of how they had been “shaped” by one another. For those from more advantaged backgrounds, this was often about confronting one’s own class privilege and snobbery – of bringing out, as charity worker Marco noted, “behaviours in me that I’m a bit ashamed of and I’m hyper-aware of now”.

For less privileged friends, diplomacy helped them to understand someone they initially saw only through the lens of privilege, and subsequently be more empathetic, while maintaining their critical stance on class inequality.

These results provide a rejoinder to economists who, in a rush to find a magic bullet to social mobility, may have passed over the complexities of cross-class friendship. It’s not just about the creation of these friendships, but their quality and longevity, and fostering the conditions where they can flourish.
